live_web_research.page_text: Atlassian and OpenAI expand partnership to turn enterprise knowledge into action | Signal Desk AI OpenAI Enterprise Atlassian and OpenAI expand partnership to turn enterprise knowledge into action Oct 6, 2026, 9:00 AM · OpenAI Image: OpenAI Atlassian is wiring OpenAI's newest models into Jira and Confluence context, and the payoff and the risk both live in how much organizational knowledge an agent can now act on. Why it matters Atlassian and OpenAI announced an expanded deal under which OpenAI's frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra and the GPT-5.6 series, will power agents across Atlassian's platform and its Rovo assistant. Rovo pairs those models with Atlassian's Teamwork Graph, which links people, projects, documents and decisions. The relationship runs both ways. Atlassian says more than 3,000 of its developers use Codex, and OpenAI says it will keep relying on Jira to manage critical workflows. The companies are also exploring Jira integrations that would let teams assign work to AI agents, track their progress and review results. From the desk We think this is one of the more sensible places to put an agent. Most of the drudgery in knowledge work is not writing; it is assembling. OpenAI's example is a product manager asking whether a launch is on track and getting an answer drawn from Jira tickets, Confluence pages and discussions, with blockers and missed milestones flagged. If that works reliably, it saves real hours, and it grounds the model in a company's own records instead of the open web. The concern is the same feature seen from the other side. A context layer that connects everything is also a context layer that exposes everything. The announcement says ChatGPT and Codex connect to project data subject to appropriate permissions, and that matters enormously. Permission systems in large companies are often messy, and an agent that can summarize across them will surface whatever those permissions get wrong, faster and more confidently than any human browsing would. The longer arc is the part we're watching most. Assigning Jira tickets to agents, then measuring their impact on cycle time through Atlassian's DX productivity platform, is a recipe for managing AI like a workforce. The companies say humans stay in control. In practice, once agent throughput becomes a dashboard metric, pressure builds to hand over more work and review less of it. That's where quality slips and accountability blurs. Our read: useful, grounded, and likely to spread quickly through teams already living in Jira. The guardrails that will matter are boring ones: clean permissions, clear audit trails of what an agent did, and review steps that don't get skipped when the metrics look good. Context The collaboration began in 2023. Atlassian has also launched plugins that bring Jira work items, Confluence content and people into ChatGPT and Codex prompts, along with CLI plugins for the Teamwork Graph. Who feels it Jira and Confluence customers Rovo gains newer OpenAI models for status checks, summaries and recommended next steps grounded in company data. Software developers Codex can pull relevant tickets and documentation through Atlassian plugins while writing and shipping code. IT and security teams Permission hygiene becomes critical as agents gain the ability to search and act across connected work data. Engineering leaders Proposed DX measurement could quantify AI's effect on cycle time, and invite pressure to automate more. Dill , Clark Barrett View a PDF of the paper titled An AI Approach to Verified Production Cryptographic Libraries, by Chuyue Sun and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Cryptographic code is critical infrastructure that must be correct, yet formally verifying production libraries remains difficult. Existing language-model proof systems solve isolated obligations with specifications and premises already given, leaving production-library verification unresolved. We present CryptoProver, an AI-based system that synthesizes internal specifications and Verus-checked proofs from high-level API contracts. Without changing executable code, CryptoProver constructs a new independent proof of curve25519-dalek and verifies RustCrypto's previously unverified chacha20 implementation against an RFC 8439 specification. These cryptographic lineages underpin deployed systems including Signal and Shadowsocks; Signal has an estimated 218M global downloads. The original developers report a focused five-month, three-person effort to verify curve25519-dalek. Given the API contracts and a fixed trusted library of field specifications, arithmetic facts, axioms, and vstd, CryptoProver synthesizes the internal specifications and proofs in 11.4 hours with USD 466.99 in recorded API cost. CryptoProver follows a trust-first design principle: mechanical gates reject specification weakening, invented axioms, and cross-module breakage, while isolation blocks reference proof retrieval, including from git history. An AI Approach to Verified Production Cryptographic Libraries Published 2 Aug 2026 in cs.CR and cs.AI | (2608.00965v1) Abstract: Cryptographic code is critical infrastructure that must be correct, yet formally verifying production libraries remains difficult. Existing language-model proof systems solve isolated obligations with specifications and premises already given, leaving production-library verification unresolved. We present CryptoProver, an AI-based system that synthesizes internal specifications and Verus-checked proofs from high-level API contracts. Without changing executable code, CryptoProver constructs a new independent proof of curve25519-dalek and verifies RustCrypto's previously unverified chacha20 implementation against an RFC 8439 specification. These cryptographic lineages underpin deployed systems including Signal and Shadowsocks; Signal has an estimated 218M global downloads. The independent, human-led curve25519-dalek verification was developed publicly over eight months by five main contributors. Given the API contracts and a fixed trusted library of field specifications, arithmetic facts, axioms, and vstd, CryptoProver synthesizes the internal specifications and proofs in 11.4 hours with USD 466.99 in recorded API cost. CryptoProver follows a trust-first design principle: mechanical gates reject specification weakening, invented axioms, and cross-module breakage, while isolation blocks reference proof retrieval, including from git history. An Integrative Review of AI Sovereignty and Collective Learning Capacity, by Kim Phuc Tran View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI sovereignty is commonly associated with control over data, infrastructure and technological dependencies. This integrative review examines how institutions convert those resources into capabilities that remain accountable and open to revision. It brings together 72 references on digital sovereignty, absorptive capacity, innovation systems and sociotechnical governance, using six reading dimensions: subject, object, scale, mechanism, legitimacy and evidence. The synthesis proposes five conditions of collective learning capacity: recognizing and retaining knowledge, transmitting it across institutions, protecting consequential challenge, authorizing correction and preserving feasible alternatives. Authoritative corrigibility connects corrective evidence to decision authority; retained option value concerns the practical alternatives that survive a technological commitment. Comparisons of the United States, China and France within Europe distinguish resources and formal arrangements from documented operation and corrective outcomes. Building on this review, Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) organizes a descriptive analysis of OECD, IMF and World Bank indicators around information resources, absorption and institutional coordination. The indicators show different resource profiles and trajectories, while leaving the operation of correction and feasible exit largely unmeasured. HCLM connects these observations to questions for institutional investigation; its national-level parameters are not estimated. Purposeful source selection, uneven case coverage and aggregate measurement constrain the conclusions. The resulting research agenda combines reproducible indicator analysis with decision-level evidence of learning, correction and retained choice. Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM), recently proposed as a dynamical framework for entropy-regulated representation learning ( Tran, 2026 ) , is used as a conceptual and diagnostic lens for interpreting national AI development as a controlled balance between information injection, absorptive capacity, and institutional dissipation. Institutional dissipation refers primarily to avoidable or poorly designed frictions such as administrative overload, coordination failures, energy bottlenecks, regulatory uncertainty, talent mobility pressures, and limited industrial absorption. Importantly, regulation is not treated here as mere friction: adaptive governance, trusted data spaces, and safety-oriented standards may increase long-term learning capacity by improving evaluation, interoperability and confidence in use. It offers a formal heuristic, policy indicators, illustrative scenarios and applications to the French setting, complemented by OECD, IMF and World Bank descriptive analyses. The numerical material separates source-based structural observations, previously reported illustrative scenario endpoints and a fully specified public-goods example. The proposed viewpoint reframes AI policy as the coordination of an open learning system whose empirical validity must be tested with historical and cross-country data. It is becoming a structural force acting on productivity, employment, education, energy, sovereignty, scientific research, and public administration. The French Commission on Artificial Intelligence, co-chaired by Philippe Aghion and Anne Bouverot, proposed 25 recommendations in 2024 to help France benefit from the AI transformation, including investment, compute capacity, talent development, and simplification of research and innovation conditions ( Commission de l’Intelligence Artificielle, 2024 ; Gouvernement français, 2024 ) . France has also announced a large AI investment agenda, including data centers and the objective of training more AI talent ( Reuters, 2025 ) . These initiatives indicate that AI has become a national development question rather than a sectoral issue. The following analysis brings these dimensions into a common analytical framework. Compute is discussed separately from education; regulation separately from innovation; sovereignty separately from industrial adoption; and energy separately from model scaling. This separation creates a conceptual challenge. A national AI strategy is not simply the sum of GPUs, data centers, startups, university programs, and legal constraints. It is a learning system : a collective mechanism by which a country generates, absorbs, transforms, regulates, and deploys knowledge. This paper proposes to analyze France as a national AI learning system through the lens of Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM), a recently proposed dynamical and information-theoretic framework for entropy-regulated representation learning ( Tran, 2026 ) . In its original machine-learning setting, HCLM is used to reason about the balance between task-driven information and entropy control. Here, that intuition is used cautiously and metaphorically at the macro-policy level. A neural network learns when useful information is injected into representations and harmful or excessive complexity is dissipated. A country develops AI capacity when useful knowledge, talent, capital, compute, data, and industrial experimentation are injected into the ecosystem, while institutional entropy—administrative complexity, organizational coordination friction, uncertainty, talent mobility pressures, regulatory transition costs, and limits in absorption capacity—is constructively managed. The aim is explicitly not to claim that a national economy literally obeys the same equations as a neural network. Rather, the HCLM analogy provides a disciplined conceptual language for policy design. It makes visible a principle that is often implicit in innovation economics: scale matters, but scale interacts with absorptive capacity, coordination, resource use, and continuity of access. The framework should be evaluated against established approaches in innovation economics, national innovation systems, public policy, and econometric analysis rather than used as a substitute for them. Its immediate contribution is conceptual and diagnostic; its stronger policy use requires empirical validation. Source-based indicators below provide descriptive structural context. Constructed scores and simulations expose modeling assumptions; they do not establish causal effects. An Integrative Review of AI Sovereignty and Collective Learning Capacity Kim Phuc Tran 20 October 2026 Abstract AI sovereignty is commonly associated with control over data, infrastructure and technological dependencies. This integrative review examines how institutions convert those resources into capabilities that remain accountable and open to revision. It brings together 72 references on digital sovereignty, absorptive capacity, innovation systems and sociotechnical governance, using six reading dimensions: subject, object, scale, mechanism, legitimacy and evidence. The synthesis proposes five conditions of collective learning capacity: recognizing and retaining knowledge, transmitting it across institutions, protecting consequential challenge, authorizing correction and preserving feasible alternatives. Authoritative corrigibility connects corrective evidence to decision authority; retained option value concerns the practical alternatives that survive a technological commitment. Comparisons of the United States, China and France within Europe distinguish resources and formal arrangements from documented operation and corrective outcomes. Building on this review, Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) organizes a descriptive analysis of OECD, IMF and World Bank indicators around information resources, absorption and institutional coordination. The indicators show different resource profiles and trajectories, while leaving the operation of correction and feasible exit largely unmeasured. HCLM connects these observations to questions for institutional investigation; its national-level parameters are not estimated. Purposeful source selection, uneven case coverage and aggregate measurement constrain the conclusions. The resulting research agenda combines reproducible indicator analysis with decision-level evidence of learning, correction and retained choice. 1 Univ. Lille, ENSAIT, ULR 2461 – GEMTEX – Génie et Matériaux Textiles, F-59000 Lille, France 2 International Chair in Data Science & Explainable Artificial Intelligence, International Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation, Dong A University, Da Nang, Vietnam Correspondence: kim-phuc.tran@ensait.fr Keywords: AI sovereignty; collective learning capacity; absorptive capacity; institutional learning; HCLM; AI governance 1 Introduction: what does sovereignty enable? National AI strategies increasingly cite domestic models, public compute infrastructure, and locally hosted cloud services as evidence of sovereignty. Assessing these claims requires knowing who sets a system’s purpose, which parts of its technical stack are supplied or governed elsewhere, and whether a ministry can evaluate performance independently of the supplier. It also requires examining the means available to workers, citizens and local authorities to contest harmful uses. When technology, evidence or public purposes change, who can revise the decision to deploy? An inventory of national assets leaves these questions unanswered. The emphasis on assets reflects substantial material constraints. Advanced chips, data centers, foundation models, research talent and patient capital are expensive, geographically concentrated and exposed to geopolitical pressure. Cloud contracts and proprietary interfaces raise switching costs; export controls or supply disruptions can remove options with little warning. Territorial ownership therefore provides only part of the capacity needed for practical autonomy. A domestically hosted model may depend on externally supplied chips, toolchains or updates. Regulators may have strong legal powers and too few qualified staff to exercise them. Research excellence may fail to reach the firms or public services expected to use it. This gap between possession and use is the conversion problem examined here. Sovereignty has several meanings in the literature. Digital-sovereignty studies use it to describe state authority, industrial autonomy, personal self-determination, and collective control over infrastructure or data (Couture and Toupin 2019; Pohle and Thiel 2020; Hummel et al. 2021). Technology-sovereignty research examines the room governments retain for action within interdependent systems (Edler et al. 2023). Roberts (2024) asks whether control is legitimate. Mügge (2024) considers who benefits when reliance on non-European platforms falls: citizens, European firms, or public institutions. A single sovereignty score would obscure the differences among these claims. Existing reviews by Hummel et al. (2021) and Fratini et al. (2024) map these uses of sovereignty. This critical integrative review asks how strategic resources become a publicly accountable capacity that can operate amid external dependence and institutional disagreement. Sovereignty scholarship addresses control and authority; work on absorptive capacity and national innovation systems explains how knowledge becomes useful; sociotechnical governance examines the institutions and affected groups involved in its use. Reading these fields together provides an account of conversion that each develops only in part. The review examines competing definitions of AI sovereignty, the institutions that turn technological resources into usable capability, and the evidence of durable public capacity in the United States, China and France within Europe. Six reading dimensions organize the comparison: subject, object, scale, mechanism, legitimacy and evidence. Collective learning capacity connects these accounts by examining how institutions retain and share knowledge, protect consequential challenge, act on reasons for revision and preserve feasible alternatives. These decisions span institutions with disputed purposes and unequal power, extending the problem beyond a bounded organization pursuing a managerial objective. The theoretical contribution links knowledge acquisition to the authority and practical means needed to revise an existing commitment. Authoritative corrigibility concerns whether relevant evidence can reach a body empowered to require a response and implement correction. Retained option value concerns whether a technically, contractually and organizationally feasible alternative remains available. Together, these concepts specify how knowledge absorption can support accountable changes in public technological commitments. The United States, China and France within Europe illustrate different institutional arrangements for this conversion. Extensive US private investment and research capacity coexist with concentrated infrastructure markets. China combines industrial accumulation and national coordination with implementation at several levels. Publicly available English-language evidence covers Chinese finance, implementation and feedback unevenly. In France, EU regulation, markets and shared infrastructure shape national implementation. The comparison examines these arrangements within the periods and institutional settings covered by the sources. The paper first develops the review and its theoretical synthesis. Section 2 explains the corpus and reading method; Sections 3 and 4 develop the literature synthesis and collective learning capacity; Section 5 compares the three institutional settings. Section 6 then introduces HCLM as an analytical extension of that foundation. Section 7 applies it to sourced indicators, followed by public-value considerations, implementation proposals and a research agenda. 2 Review design and interpretive strategy 2.1 Review design and corpus The study combines a critical integrative review with a descriptive analysis of published indicators. The review relates concepts and explanatory arguments across digital sovereignty, absorptive capacity, innovation systems and sociotechnical governance (Whittemore and Knafl 2005; Torraco 2005; Snyder 2019). It develops an institutional account of AI sovereignty and applies the same analytical questions to the United States, China and France within Europe. HCLM then provides a framework for organizing the indicator analysis. The literature synthesis and numerical calculations have distinct evidential roles. The selected corpus contains 72 references: 39 journal articles, including conceptual essays and commentaries, 11 books, nine institutional reports, five legal or policy instruments, three methodological sources, three datasets and two conference papers. These inventory categories are mutually exclusive, with methodological articles classified by their role. The accompanying inventory records one entry per reference, its source type, analytical role and use in the manuscript. Its primary-role labels comprise 36 conceptual or theoretical sources, 24 sources used for case evidence, eight used for indicator interpretation or data, three review-method sources and one HCLM background work. These labels describe how references contribute to the argument; they do not count independent empirical studies. The retained works contribute definitions of sovereignty, explanations of dependency or institutional capability, comparisons of strategies and institutions, or evidence about implementation and public accountability. A source may inform one question without addressing the others. Methodological works support the review design. Legal records and datasets support the particular institutional or descriptive claims for which they are cited. The forthcoming HCLM book provides the background for the institutional adaptation developed in Section 6 and used to organize the indicator analysis in Section 7. Its role remains distinct from the sources documenting national institutions and observations. 2.2 Source interpretation and synthesis The source is the inventory unit, while the substantive claim is the unit of comparison. Six dimensions organize the source map. Subject identifies who claims, exercises or contests control. Object identifies the resource, service or decision concerned. Scale locates the claim at organizational, national, regional or cross-border level. Mechanism records the proposed or observed process through which control or capability operates. Legitimacy records the justification of authority and the rights or interests involved. Evidence identifies the kind and scope of support available for the claim. Multiple actors and scales can be retained, while fields outside a source’s remit limit its interpretation. A source-level row summarizes its analytical use; it is not a transcript of every passage or claim. Appraisal is qualitative and specific to the claim. Conceptual arguments are considered in relation to their assumptions and explanatory scope; empirical findings in relation to their settings and designs; official records in relation to their date and institutional remit; and datasets in relation to their definitions, coverage and comparability. The inventory distinguishes a source’s evidential basis from the interpretation developed in the manuscript. For example, an administrative announcement establishes a mandate, whereas an implementation evaluation supplies evidence about operation within its remit. Tracing a challenge through an authorized response and implemented correction requires records of the relevant decisions. The synthesis is organized around comparisons within and across the literature clusters. Absorptive-capacity and innovation-system accounts inform recognition, retention and transmission of knowledge. Accountability and sociotechnical research inform protected challenge and authorized correction. Work on dependence and switching constraints informs feasible alternatives. These connections motivate the five conditions of collective learning capacity. Auth
